query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy protective coatings, friction-induced microstructural reorganization—specifically, the dynamic formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline (or nano-amorphous) surface layer—governs wear performance by increasing local hardness and reducing friction, thereby lowering the wear rate.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating with a relatively coarse-grained microstructure deposited by methods such as atmospheric plasma spraying.
generation.intervention: Pre-treat the coating to suppress or delay friction-induced dynamic microstructural evolution (for example, via an annealing or surface hardening step that stabilizes the initial grain structure) compared to an untreated baseline.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests under controlled loads and speeds in a low-oxidation (inert) or moderately oxidizing environment to isolate the mechanical rather than chemical contributions.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of an ultra-nanocrystalline or dynamically amorphized near-surface layer during sliding contact, as evidenced by reduced grain sizes and/or amorphous features in worn surfaces.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, shear forces induce a microstructural transformation at the coating surface. The transition from a coarse grain to an ultra-nanocrystalline (or partially amorphous) state enhances surface hardness and accommodates plastic deformation via grain-boundary-mediated mechanisms, effectively suppressing material removal and reducing friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Treated coatings that inhibit the formation of the adaptive ultra-nanocrystalline layer will show higher friction coefficients and increased wear rates relative to untreated coatings where dynamic reorganization can occur. In untreated coatings, post-test analysis should reveal a near-surface layer with nanoscale grain sizes correlated with superior wear resistance.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited, coarse-grained high-entropy alloy coating that is free to undergo friction-induced microstructural evolution during wear testing.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under moderate sliding loads and speeds, primarily in conditions where oxidation is either minimized or plays a secondary role relative to mechanical deformation. Extreme conditions (very high loads, temperatures, or highly oxidizing environments) may invoke additional mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The extent to which chemical effects (such as oxidation) interact with the mechanical dynamic amorphization process is not fully defined, and the relative contributions of grain refinement versus oxide nanocomposite formation in reactive environments require further elucidation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy coatings: one set as-deposited (expected to undergo dynamic surface reorganization during wear) and a second set that has been pre-annealed or otherwise processed to stabilize the coarse-grained structure and inhibit further grain refinement. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests under controlled load, speed, and environmental conditions.
measurements: Post-test surface microstructure analysis via TEM/SEM to measure near-surface grain size and phase characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated coatings (designed to inhibit dynamic surface nanostructuring) exhibit wear rates and friction coefficients similar to or lower than those of the as-deposited samples—in spite of clear suppression of microstructural transition—then the hypothesis that friction-induced dynamic formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer controls wear performance would be falsified.

Initial Oxidation Behavior of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Coating Produced by Atmospheric Plasma Spraying in the Range of 650 °C to 1000 °C

Abstract: AbstractAs protective coatings for the thermal parts of aero-engines, AlCoCrFeNi coatings have good application prospects. In this study, atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) was used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy coatings (HECs), which were oxidized from 650 °C to 1000 °C. The mechanism of the oxide layer formation and the internal phase transition were systematically investigated. The results show that a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure was formed at the initial stage of oxidation. The redistribution of elements and phase transition occurred in the HECs’ matrix; the BCC/B2 structure transformed to Al-Ni ordered B2 phase and Fe-Cr disordered A2 phase.Keywords: plasma spraying, oxidation behavior, high-entropy coatings, phase transition

Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Reactive wear protection through strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces

Abstract: Wear-related energy and material loss cost over 2500 Billion Euro per year. Traditional wisdom suggests that high-strength materials reveal low wear rates, yet, their plastic deformation mechanisms also influence their wear performance. High strength and homogeneous deformation behavior, which allow accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture, are crucial for developing wear-resistant metals. Here, we present an approach to achieve superior wear resistance via in-situ formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface during wear, by reaction of the metal surface with its oxidative environment, a principle that we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. We design a TiNbZr-Ag alloy that forms an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer upon dry sliding. The strong (2.4 GPa yield strength) and deformable (homogeneous deformation to 20% strain) nanocomposite surface reduces the wear rate of the TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude. The reactive wear protection strategy offers a pathway for designing ultra-wear resistant alloys
